Citizenship
SIT-ih-zen-ship
noun
From Old French citeain (later citoyen), from cite (“city”), derived from Latin civitas (“community of citizens, city-state”), itself from civis (“citizen”). The suffix -ship denotes the status, condition, or rights belonging to a member of a civic body. In New Testament usage the Greek politeuma (“colony, enrolled community”) carries the sense of a people who hold the rights and identity of a distant city while residing in foreign territory.

Biblical Definition

The citizenship of the believer is heavenly and permanent. Paul's definitive declaration in Philippians 3:20 states it with striking force: “Our citizenship is in heaven — from which we also eagerly wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.” The Greek politeuma denotes an enrolled colony — a community of people who carry the rights and constitution of a distant city while residing in a foreign land. The Philippians, as proud citizens of a Roman colony, would have grasped the register instantly: the church is a colony of heaven, living under heaven's law in the midst of a foreign jurisdiction. Paul grounds this in Ephesians 2:19: the Gentile converts once described as “strangers and aliens” are now “fellow citizens with the saints, and members of God's household.” The barrier is broken, the registry is changed, and they belong to a commonwealth that transcends every earthly polis. The heavenly city toward which the church journeys is described in Revelation 21:27 as admitting only those whose names are written in the Lamb's book of life — citizenship is covenantal and determined, not meritocratic or self-achieved. Paul's allegory in Galatians 4:26 identifies the church with the “Jerusalem above,” which is “free” — a city whose citizens are not born into bondage but into liberty. Reformed covenant theology frames this heavenly citizenship as the fulfilment of Israel's calling: a holy nation, a royal priesthood, dwelling in the city of the living God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster defines citizenship as the condition or status of being a citizen; the rights, privileges, and duties belonging to a member of a city or state. In its theological register it names the believer's enrolled membership in the heavenly commonwealth.

expand to see more

CITIZENSHIP, n. [citizen and ship.] 1. The state of being vested with the rights and privileges of a citizen. 2. The condition of belonging to a civil community with its attendant rights and duties. 3. The quality of conduct befitting a citizen; civic virtue and participation. 4. Legal membership in a state or nation, conferring full civic rights.

CITIZEN, n. [Old Fr. citeain; from cite, a city.] 1. A native or naturalized person who owes allegiance to a government and is entitled to its protection. 2. An inhabitant of a city. 3. In the ecclesiastical sense of Eph 2:19 and Phil 3:20: one whose name is enrolled in the registry of the heavenly city and whose primary obligation is to its King.

Key Scripture

Phil 3:20 — "For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:"

Eph 2:19 — "Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;"

Gal 4:26 — "But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all."

Rev 21:27 — "And there shall in no wise enter into it any thing that defileth, neither whatsoever worketh abomination, or maketh a lie: but they which are written in the Lamb's book of life."

Modern Corruption

Progressive theology conflates heavenly citizenship with earthly civic activism, reducing the Pauline politeuma to a mandate for political engagement rather than a declaration of the believer's primary and permanent identity.

expand to see more

The contemporary social-gospel reading of Philippians 3:20 inverts the apostle's argument. Paul's point is that Christian citizenship is not primarily in the earthly city — and that this heavenly identity relativizes and detaches the believer from the idols of earthly political belonging. The progressive reading converts the verse into a mandate for political activism: because we are citizens of the kingdom of God, we must work to make the earthly city conform to kingdom values. The heavenly is collapsed into the social, and “eagerly waiting for a Savior” becomes working for a movement.

The Westminster Confession (chs. 25–26) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (ch. 26) consistently distinguish the church as a spiritual community from any earthly political order. Heavenly citizenship does not abolish legitimate civil participation, but it subordinates all earthly loyalties. The believer's primary identification is with the city whose foundations are eternal, and his posture toward all earthly cities is that of a resident alien — engaged but not assimilated, involved but not idolizing. The registry is the Lamb's book of life (Rev 21:27), not any earthly voter roll or party membership.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rooted in Latin civitas (“city, community of citizens”) and Greek politeuma (“colony, enrolled community with the rights of a distant city”) — the believer's registered membership in the eternal commonwealth of the saints.

expand to see more

Latin civis — citizen; civitas — city-state, community of citizens; root of ‘civil,’ ‘civic,’ ‘civilization’

Greek politeuma — a colony of citizens; an enrolled community carrying the rights and constitution of a distant polis (Phil 3:20)

Greek politeia — citizenship, constitution; the rights and condition of belonging to a city or commonwealth

Hebrew qahal — assembly, gathered community; the Old Testament covenant congregation as the antetype of the heavenly city

Ephesians 2:19 — “fellow citizens with the saints” — Paul's proclamation that Gentile inclusion is not second-class but full membership

Usage

"The believer's heavenly citizenship is not an escapist fantasy but a clarifying identity — knowing where he finally belongs frees him from the anxious need to secure his place in any earthly order or political coalition."

"Reformed mission theology draws on Philippians 3:20 to distinguish the church from a political party: the church is a colony of heaven, not an arm of any earthly government, and her constitution is the Word of God."

"The imagery of the “Jerusalem above” in Galatians 4:26 connects heavenly citizenship to the covenant of grace — membership in the heavenly city is not by natural birth but by the Spirit's new birth from above."
